title: Where are you from?
goal: Say where you're from, where you live, what you do, and which languages you speak — while setting up the two verb groups with the most members and two ways of asking a yes/no question.
bekal: answer *Odakle si?* and *Gdje živiš?* in full sentences
use verbs of the *-am* and *-im* groups in all six forms
negate with *ne* and ask questions with both *da li* and *li*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Odakle si?
dialogs.intro: Budi's first coffee break at the office. Amina is curious, and like almost every Bosnian, she asks straight out without beating around the bush.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: Budi, where are you from? From Malaysia?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ne, nisam. Iz Indonezije sam, iz Jakarte.
lines.id: No. I'm from Indonesia, from Jakarta.
lines.literal: no, I-am-not. from Indonesia-gen I-am, from Jakarta-gen.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: Oh! And where do you live now?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Živim u Sarajevu, u Starom Gradu. A ti?
lines.id: I live in Sarajevo, in Stari Grad. And you?
lines.literal: I-live in Sarajevo-loc, in Old-Town-loc. and you?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Ja sam iz Mostara, ali radim ovdje već tri godine.
lines.id: I'm from Mostar, but I've been working here for three years.
lines.literal: I I-am from Mostar-gen, but I-work here already three years-gen.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: What do you do at the company?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Programerka sam, kao i ti. A koje jezike govoriš?
lines.id: I'm a programmer, just like you. And which languages do you speak?
lines.literal: programmer-f I-am, like also you. and which-pl languages-pl you-speak?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Govorim indonežanski, engleski i malo bosanski.
lines.id: I speak Indonesian, English, and a little Bosnian.
lines.literal: I-speak indonesian, english and little bosnian.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: You speak really well! Do you understand everything?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ne razumijem sve, ali učim svaki dan.
lines.id: Not everything, but I study every day.
lines.literal: not I-understand everything, but I-study every day.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I don't know. What does it mean?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: To je glavna čaršija — turska riječ za pijacu. Idemo sutra!
lines.id: It's the main bazaar — a Turkish word for market. Let's go tomorrow!
lines.literal: that it-is main-f bazaar — turkish-f word for market-acc. we-go tomorrow!

notes: ***Odakle si?* is answered with *iz* + a changed ending.** The place name changes its ending: *Indonezija → iz Indonezije*, *Jakarta → iz Jakarte*, *Mostar → iz Mostara*. That form is called the genitive and gets its full treatment in unit 8. For now just learn the pattern: names ending in *-a* switch to *-e*, names ending in a consonant add *-a*.

**Saying "no" takes two words.** *Ne* on its own sounds very short, almost curt. The natural thing is to repeat the verb in the negative: *Ne, nisam.* — *Ne, ne znam.* — *Ne, ne živim tamo.* Much like English "No, I'm not" or "No, I don't" — and it works for every yes/no question in Bosnian.

**Language names are lowercase, country names capitalized.** *Bosna* but *bosanski*; *Indonezija* but *indonežanski*; *Engleska* but *engleski*. Nationalities are capitalized: *Bosanac, Indonežanin*. This is the opposite of English for language names — watch out when writing.

***Radim ovdje već tri godine* — present tense, not past.** English says "I have been working here for three years", but Bosnian uses the **present tense** for something that started in the past and is still going on. The key word is *već* (already). Don't be tempted to use the past here — it would mean "I once worked here".

**Baščaršija.** The name of the heart of Sarajevo's old town, from Turkish *baş* (head, main) + *çarşı* (market). Hundreds of words like this live on in everyday Bosnian: *sapun* (soap), *sat* (hour, clock), *šećer* (sugar), *insan* (human being), *selam*, *dunjaluk* (the world). Some even reached English through the same route: *kafa* (coffee), *jogurt*, *kiosk*.

grammars.title: Present tense — the two biggest groups
body: Bosnian verbs change for the person — six forms in each tense, just like *biti* in unit 1. The good news: the endings are nearly uniform. All that separates the groups is **the vowel before the ending** and **the *oni* form**.
after: **The endings are the same in both groups: *-m, -š, —, -mo, -te*.** Only the vowel in front differs: the **-am** group (*znam, znaš*) and the **-im** group (*radim, radiš*). The *on/ona* form never has an ending at all — just cut the *-m* off the *ja* form.

**The *oni* form is the one you can't guess**: the *-am* group uses **-aju** (*znaju, imaju, pitaju*), the *-im* group uses **-e** (*rade, govore, žive*). This is the only row you must learn separately.

**The dictionary form is often misleading.** *Raditi* and *živjeti* look different, but both belong to the *-im* group. *Znati* and *imati* belong to the *-am* group. That's why this course always lists verbs in their **ja form**, not the dictionary form — that's the form that actually tells you the group. The third group (*-em*: *pišem, idem, zovem*) comes in unit 6.
**The pronoun is dropped unless stressed.** *Govorim bosanski* can only mean "I speak Bosnian". *Ja govorim bosanski* means "*I* speak Bosnian" — there's a hidden contrast in it.

grammars.title: Saying no and asking questions
body: Two tools you'll use in every unit from now on, and both are simpler than you'd expect.
after: **Negating: *ne* before the verb, written separately.** *Ne znam. Ne razumijem. Ne živim u Mostaru.* No helper like English *do* — just *ne*. Only three verbs fuse their negative into one word, and all three are very common: *nisam* (from *biti*), *nemam* (from *imati*), *neću* (from *htjeti*, to want).

**Yes/no questions have two equally correct forms.** First, *da li* at the front: **Da li** *govoriš bosanski?* Second, *li* slipped in after the verb: *Govoriš* **li** *bosanski?* Both are everyday Bosnian; the second is a little shorter and more common in writing. With *biti*, the long form is used: *Jesi li umoran?*, *Jeste li Vi profesor?*

**No need for "do" or swapping words around.** Unlike English, a Bosnian question can be exactly the same as a statement — just raise your voice at the end: *Ti si student?* is a valid and very common question.
**Question words always come first.** *Gdje živiš?*, *Šta radiš?*, *Koliko košta?* — just as in English.

blocks.text: Country, person, and language are always three different words in Bosnian, even where English uses one word for two of them ("Japanese" = the person and the language). Once you see the pattern, you can guess the rest.

Language names **always end in *-ski* and are always lowercase**. If you know the country, you can almost always work out the language yourself. To say "in Bosnian", use *na*: *Kako se to kaže na bosanskom?*

blocks.title: From where — and where
items: **Origin: *iz* + genitive ending.** *Ja sam iz Indonezije. On je iz Mostara. Oni su iz Njemačke.* Names ending in *-a* change it to *-e*; names ending in a consonant add *-a*.
**Where you live: *u* + locative ending.** *Živim u Sarajevu. Ona živi u Jakarti. Oni žive u Njemačkoj.* The ending is *-u* for masculine and neuter words, *-i* for feminine words.

**For now, learn whole sentences, not tables.** These two endings each have their own unit — the genitive in unit 8, the locative in unit 9 — and there it will all click at once. What matters today: your ear has heard that place names *do change*, so it won't come as a shock later.

blocks.text: The question comes in two equally common forms: *Šta si po zanimanju?* ("what are you by occupation?") and *Čime se baviš?* ("with what do you occupy yourself?"). The answer has no article: *Programer sam* — "I'm a programmer", with no *a*.

The pattern is almost always the same: the feminine form adds **-ica** or **-ka** to the masculine. If you forget the feminine, using the masculine won't cause any misunderstanding — but the feminine sounds far more natural, and in Bosnia it is almost always used.

Three phrases that help when you don't have a neat answer yet: *Tražim posao* (I'm looking for work), *Ne radim* (I'm not working), *Studiram* (I'm at university). And one sentence you'll often need in Sarajevo: *Radim za jednu firmu iz Indonezije* — I work for a company from Indonesia.
